title: 1 Samuel 28:3–14
context: Samuel is dead, and Saul, terrified by the Philistine army and receiving no answer from the LORD, disguises himself and consults a medium at Endor, which the Law forbids. The narrator says the woman saw Samuel. Interpreters across traditions read the appearance as a genuine one by God’s permission, a demonic impersonation, or the medium’s trickery; the text does not describe how it happened.

verses.text: Now Samuel was dead, and all Israel had mourned for him and buried him in Ramah, even in his own city. Saul had sent away those who had familiar spirits and the wizards out of the land.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel is dead and buried in Ramah, and Saul had sent away mediums and wizards. Arminian readers see background that prepares for Saul contradicting his own earlier obedience to the Law.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the scene set with care. Deuteronomy 18:10–12 forbids such practices, and the narrator’s reminder about Samuel’s death frames everything that follows at Endor.

verses.text: The Philistines gathered themselves together, and came and encamped in Shunem; and Saul gathered all Israel together, and they encamped in Gilboa.
verses.arminianNotes: The Philistines camp at Shunem, and Saul gathers Israel at Gilboa. Arminian readers see the armies arranged for a decisive battle in which Saul’s reign will be tested to the breaking point.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the stage set for the battle reported in chapter 31. The geographical notes make the danger concrete and show Israel facing a formidable enemy.

verses.text: When Saul saw the army of the Philistines, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly.
verses.arminianNotes: Seeing the Philistine army, Saul is afraid and “his heart trembled greatly.” Arminian readers see fear in a king who has drifted from God and lost confidence in his help.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see deep fear in a king from whom the LORD’s Spirit had departed in chapter 16. Readers in both traditions note the contrast with David’s earlier courage before Goliath.

verses.text: When Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD didn’t answer him by dreams, by Urim, or by prophets.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul inquires of the LORD, but the LORD does not answer “by dreams, by Urim, or by prophets.” Arminian readers see silence as a consequence of Saul’s persistent disobedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God withholding guidance as judgment. 1 Chronicles 10:13–14 also comments on Saul’s end, and interpreters explain the relation between that summary and this verse in different ways.

verses.text: Then Saul said to his servants, “Seek for me a woman who has a familiar spirit, that I may go to her and inquire of her.” His servants said to him, “Behold, there is a woman who has a familiar spirit at Endor.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul says, “Seek for me a woman who has a familiar spirit.” His servants name a woman at Endor. Arminian readers see desperation driving Saul to the very practice he had removed from the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Saul turning from God’s appointed means to forbidden ones. The verse shows how spiritual disorder can lead someone to seek guidance where God has forbidden it.

verses.text: Saul disguised himself and put on other clothing, and went, he and two men with him, and they came to the woman by night. Then he said, “Please consult for me by the familiar spirit, and bring me up whomever I shall name to you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul disguises himself and goes by night, asking, “Please consult for me by the familiar spirit.” Arminian readers see the disguise and darkness as signs that Saul knows he is doing wrong.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see secrecy surrounding a forbidden act. The narrator emphasizes concealment, and the request to “bring me up whomever I shall name” sets up the encounter without explaining any method.

verses.text: The woman said to him, “Behold, you know what Saul has done, how he has cut off those who have familiar spirits and the wizards out of the land. Why then do you lay a snare for my life, to cause me to die?”
verses.arminianNotes: The woman says, “Why then do you lay a snare for my life, to cause me to die?” Arminian readers see her fear of the penalties Saul himself had enforced against her practice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the irony that she reminds the disguised king of his own decree. Her suspicion shows that Saul’s policy had been known and feared throughout the land.

verses.text: Saul swore to her by the LORD, saying, “As the LORD lives, no punishment will happen to you for this thing.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul swears, “As the LORD lives, no punishment will happen to you for this thing.” Arminian readers see the tragic irony of Saul invoking the LORD’s name to protect a forbidden practice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Saul misusing an oath by the LORD. The verse captures the confusion of a king who still uses religious language while acting against God’s law.

verses.text: Then the woman said, “Whom shall I bring up to you?” He said, “Bring Samuel up for me.”
verses.arminianNotes: The woman asks, “Whom shall I bring up to you?” Saul answers, “Bring Samuel up for me.” Arminian readers see Saul seeking the prophet whose warnings he had ignored while Samuel lived.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Saul reaching for the voice he had rejected. The request shows his desperation, and the narrator offers no explanation of how the medium intended to proceed.

verses.text: When the woman saw Samuel, she cried with a loud voice; and the woman spoke to Saul, saying, “Why have you deceived me? For you are Saul!”
verses.arminianNotes: “When the woman saw Samuel, she cried with a loud voice.” Arminian readers note that this is not a dividing line between the traditions. Interpreters in both camps have read the scene as Samuel genuinely appearing by God’s permission, as a demonic impersonation, or as the medium’s trickery. The text gives no mechanics, and these notes declare no winner.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the question as one that cuts across both traditions rather than between them. The genuine-appearance reading is widely held among readers in both traditions, and the other two readings have also been held by Christian interpreters. Those views weigh WEB’s wording “saw Samuel” differently, and the passage does not settle the matter.

verses.text: The king said to her, “Don’t be afraid! What do you see?” The woman said to Saul, “I see a god coming up out of the earth.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul says, “Don’t be afraid! What do you see?” She answers, “I see a god coming up out of the earth.” Arminian readers see her description as reported speech without technical explanation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat her words with restraint. The term she uses is reported, not explained, and readers across traditions caution against building detailed theories about the unseen world on this verse.

verses.text: He said to her, “What does he look like?” She said, “An old man comes up. He is covered with a robe.” Saul perceived that it was Samuel, and he bowed with his face to the ground, and showed respect.
verses.arminianNotes: She describes “An old man … covered with a robe,” and “Saul perceived that it was Samuel.” Arminian readers note the narrator reports Saul’s perception and his act of respect without adding explanation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the wording. Those who hold Samuel truly appeared stress the narrator’s language; those who hold an impersonation or trickery stress that the description comes through the medium and Saul’s perception.
